rv.q: Sometimes confounding and excessive, Slave Play is also funny and intelligently provocative as it examines the lingering impact of slavery through the distress and desires of characters who aren’t what they first seem.
Brash, smart and gleefully confrontational, this is the kind of show that starts arguments.
With asperity but also love, “Slave Play” lets us all see ourselves in the muddle that is race in America now.
In all of the things this play does well, I think it's best at eliciting a reaction to uneasy dynamics in some of the deepest, darkest, most generationally traumatic aspects of one's psyche.
Unfortunately, further discussion about the fruits of Antebellum Therapy never returns to the wonderful simplicity (and hilarity) of Alana’s honest evaluation of the entire process.
A second viewing of 'Slave Play' confirms that this is one of the most original, exciting, funny and thought-provoking plays seen in New York this decade — a masterpiece.
A remarkable evening full of uneasy moments that could go wrong in any single minute but pulls off an incendiary work.
It is bleak and damning, and all the more provocative for being so.
And that is what makes this the most radical (and unwaveringly confident and self-protected) Broadway play in years.
Harris’s play is full of a sharp satirical intelligence that makes the right words fall from the wrong mouths, and resists pat conclusions.
For all that, the play feels overlong, and the sense of the characters as fully developed individuals is fitful.
Meanwhile, “Slave Play” makes a kind of history of its own, boldly bringing Broadway into unfamiliar waters!

That the trauma of American slavery continues to resonate may be no surprise to more than half the country, but never has the excavation of its psychosexual consequences been so wildly entertaining and incisive.
Slave Play ventures into subject matter the likes of which this playgoer has never seen presented on Broadway, and does so in a bold, even outlandish manner that should be admired and welcomed.
Slave Play earns its laughs, but not its sorrow.
But to my mind, this Broadway transfer only confirms my initial reaction at Theatre Workshop—the emperor has no clothes.
Never mind the sex and nudity - at its core Slave Play is too obsessed with conceptual naval gazing to the extent that it forgets that its characters are human beings.
